Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- After deliberating for more than four hours, a jury convicted a Nevada man of 22 counts Tuesday for videotaping himself sexually assaulting a toddler, CNN affiliates report. Chester Arthur Stiles has been convicted of videtaping a sexual assault on a child. Chester Arthur Stiles, 38, faces a maximum sentence of life in prison. He was convicted of lewdness with a child, sexual assault with a minor, attempted sexual assault with a minor and other related charges. He showed no reaction as the verdict was read after more than four hours of jury deliberations, according to KLAS. Sentencing was set for May 8. The crime triggered a national manhunt and search for the girl when the tape surfaced in 2007. Jurors in Stiles' trial viewed the videotape, but the judge would not allow members sitting in the gallery to view it, and a screen was put up to block the jury box, said Michael Sommermeyer, spokesman for Clark County, Nevada, courts. Some members of the media were allowed to view the tape as well, but the judge did not want the reactions of reporters or the public to influence jurors, he said. The charges also related to another girl who Stiles was accused of sexually assaulting on videotape. The tape was given to authorities in September 2007 by a man who said he had found it in the desert five months before. On it, police found images of the small girl being sexually assaulted. After attempting unsuccessfully to find out the girl's identity, authorities turned to the media for help and released a picture of the girl, and the case drew nationwide attention. She was found in October 2007. An attorney for her mother said she was 7 years old and safe and healthy. The rape occurred before the girl's third birthday, while she was in the care of a baby-sitter her mother had hired, he said. The mother did not know the girl had been victimized. After the girl was found, authorities asked CNN and other news organizations to stop showing her picture. In an appearance on "The Dr. Phil Show," the girl's mother said the girl has no recollection of the assault. Stiles, a resident of Pahrump, Nevada, was arrested in a traffic stop in October 2007. Police said at the time they pulled Stiles' car over because it had no license plate, and became suspicious when the driver displayed an expired California license with a photo that did not match his appearance. Stiles eventually admitted who he was and that he was being sought, authorities said. The man who turned the tape over to authorities, Darrin Tuck, faced criminal charges because of the delay in turning it over, during which authorities alleged he showed it to others. A judge gave Tuck a one-year suspended sentence and three years of probation in April after he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to obstruct a public officer, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal. He initially had faced a felony count of possession of child pornography.

**Videotape Found in Nevada Desert Led to Arrest and Life Sentences in Child-Assault Case**

**PAHRUMP, Nev. —** A videotape discovered in the desert outside this southern Nevada town triggered a nationwide search for a child and her attacker, eventually leading authorities to Chester Arthur Stiles. But investigators also faced a disturbing question: Why had the man who found the recording waited months before giving it to police?

The case emerged publicly in 2007, when the Nye County Sheriff’s Office obtained a videotape depicting the sexual assault of a very young girl. The recording was so alarming that investigators released carefully selected, nonexplicit images in an effort to identify the child and the adult shown with her.

The appeal quickly produced results. The girl’s mother recognized her daughter, who was by then older and was found alive and safe. Investigators determined that the assault had occurred several years earlier, when the child was about 2 or 3 years old.

Attention then turned to Stiles, a former Las Vegas-area animal trainer who had been acquainted with people close to the child. Authorities said the tape and witness information connected him to the assault. A national manhunt followed, accompanied by widespread television coverage and distribution of his photograph.

Stiles was arrested in October 2007 in Henderson, near Las Vegas, after police received information about his location. He was taken into custody without the prolonged confrontation some officials had feared.

### Tape was not immediately reported

The videotape reached law enforcement through Darrin Tuck, who said he had found it in the desert near Pahrump. According to contemporary accounts, Tuck discovered the recording months before authorities received it.

Tuck said he had watched enough of the tape to understand that it showed a serious crime. Yet he did not immediately contact police.

His delay became a major part of the investigation and public controversy surrounding the case. Tuck offered explanations that included fear that police might suspect him and concern arising from his own legal circumstances. Accounts also indicated that he had discussed the tape with others and attempted to determine who was shown in it before finally taking it to authorities.

Police sharply criticized the delay, saying that immediate reporting could have allowed investigators to identify the victim and suspect sooner. Officials also examined Tuck’s account of where and how the tape had been found, although Stiles—not Tuck—was ultimately identified as the attacker shown in the recording.

The episode underscored a central concern for investigators: During the months the tape remained outside police custody, authorities did not know whether the child was still in danger or whether the person responsible might attack another child.

### Child identified and protected

Once investigators released images from the recording, the victim was identified quickly. Authorities did not publicly name her, following the standard practice of protecting the identity of a child sexual-assault victim.

The girl’s mother told investigators that Stiles had access to the child through a woman who had cared for her. Detectives then reconstructed the circumstances under which the assault had taken place and developed evidence supporting multiple felony charges.

Officials emphasized that the girl was safe when located and was no longer in contact with Stiles.

### Arrest and prosecution

Stiles was charged with numerous offenses arising from the recorded abuse. The prosecution relied heavily on the videotape, along with identification evidence and information concerning his access to the victim.

He ultimately entered guilty pleas rather than proceed through a full trial on every count. In 2009, a Nevada judge imposed multiple consecutive life sentences for sexual assault and lewdness offenses involving the child. The structure of the sentence meant that Stiles would not have a realistic opportunity for release.

At sentencing, the court described the crimes as exceptionally serious, reflecting both the age of the victim and the fact that the assault had been recorded.

### A chance discovery that left lasting questions

The physical path of the videotape—from the desert, through Tuck’s possession and finally to the sheriff’s office—remained one of the case’s most unusual elements. Authorities never treated the delay as a minor matter. For investigators, every day the recording was withheld represented time in which the victim’s identity and condition were unknown.

At the same time, the tape ultimately became the evidence that exposed a crime that might otherwise have remained hidden. Its release to police led to the child’s identification, Stiles’ capture and a prosecution ending in life sentences.

The case also prompted law-enforcement officials to repeat a basic warning: Anyone who finds evidence of child abuse should avoid copying, distributing or conducting a private investigation and should immediately contact police. Such material can be crucial evidence, and delays can place victims at further risk.

**Videotape led to nationwide hunt and conviction of Nevada child sex offender**

LAS VEGAS (AP) — A videotape discovered in Nevada triggered a nationwide search for an unidentified man, helped authorities identify a young victim and ultimately led to Chester Arthur Stiles’ conviction on multiple child sexual assault charges.

The recording, which showed a man sexually abusing a girl believed to be about 3 years old, was turned over to law enforcement after it was found near Pahrump, west of Las Vegas. Investigators initially did not know the names of either the man or the child.

Authorities later released selected, nonexplicit images of the suspect and objects visible in the recording. The images spread through national news reports and law enforcement bulletins, generating tips from across the country.

People who knew Stiles recognized him, allowing police to attach a name to the face on the tape. The publicity also helped investigators identify the girl, who was older by then and living safely with her family. Her identity was withheld because she was a minor and the victim of sexual abuse.

The search ended in October 2007, when Stiles was arrested in the Las Vegas area following a traffic stop. Prosecutors said the videotape provided central evidence, documenting the abuse and linking Stiles to the child.

Stiles was later convicted in Nevada on numerous felony counts, including sexual assault and lewdness involving a child. In 2009, he received 21 consecutive life sentences, effectively ensuring that he would spend the rest of his life in prison.

The case became a prominent example of how public distribution of carefully selected suspect images can revive an investigation when authorities do not know the identities of those shown in recorded evidence.
